Aneurysmal Bone Cyst

[THOUGHT] The case presents a classic radiographic and MRI appearance of a benign, expansile, lytic bone lesion in a young adult: “soap bubble” appearance on X-ray, well-demarcated non-invasive lesion on MRI with thin sclerotic rim and no aggressive features (no cortical destruction, no soft-tissue extension, no periosteal reaction). While Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) is in the differential—and cannot be definitively excluded on imaging alone—it is statistically less common under age 25 (peak incidence 20–40, but rare <20; ~5% occur <25), and typically shows more aggressive features (e.g., cortical thinning/breakthrough, fluid–fluid levels less prominent than in ABC, higher T2 signal heterogeneity). Critically, however, definitive diagnosis of ABC (vs. secondary ABC, GCT, chondroblastoma, or telangiectatic osteosarcoma) requires histopathology. Yet per current guidelines (e.g., AJR, Skeletal Radiol), image-based diagnosis of *primary* ABC is considered sufficiently reliable for clinical decision-making *when imaging is classic*, particularly in young patients, and biopsy is often deferred until surgical planning or if atypical features emerge. No red flags are present: no pain at rest/night, no rapid progression, no neurologic deficit, no constitutional symptoms, and imaging shows no malignancy-associated features (e.g., permeative margins, moth-eaten bone, soft-tissue mass, pathological fracture). Turn limit is 7/10 — still room for clarification, but not required unless critical uncertainty remains. Given the high specificity of the imaging triad (lytic + expansile + soap-bubble + fluid–fluid levels on MRI) in this demographic, the diagnosis of Aneurysmal Bone Cyst is clinically sufficient and appropriately prioritized.
